panels.rationale: Single contrast-enhanced coronal MRI from a case series on glomus jugulare tumor; the caption explicitly attributes the imaged lesion to glomus jugulare tumor and describes its extent to the atlas level, a characteristic enhancing skull-base/jugular bulb mass.
panels.attribution_text: Hafez et al. The safety and efficacy of gamma knife surgery in management of glomus jugulare tumor.. World journal of surgical oncology 2010. doi:10.1186/1477-7819-8-76. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Stereotactic MRI + contrast pre-gamma knife surgery for glomus jugulare tumor extends to the atlas vertebrae level.
in_text_mentions: The mean age of patients was 43.6 years (range, 22-64 years). There were 11 females and two male. The tumors were located at left side in 10 cases and right side in 3 cases (Figure 1). The most common neurological deficit was IX, X, XI cranial nerve paresis in 7 patients, sensorineural deterioration in hearing, facial paresis, XII cranial nerve paresis and trigeminal impairment were also recorded. Pulstile tinnitus was recorded in 9 cases and ataxia in 3 cases.

plate_findings.evidence: Bone window of CT scan showing an extremely widened right side jugular foramen (depicted by the orange arrow of Figure 4)
with a characteristic “moth-eaten” pattern (depicted by blue arrow of Figure 4) of destruction of petrous part of temporal bone

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial bone-window CT of the skull base with a blue arrow marking the moth-eaten permeative destruction of the petrous temporal bone adjacent to the widened right jugular foramen, the classic osseous manifestation of a glomus jugulare paraganglioma. B: Coronal bone-window CT reconstruction of the skull base belonging to the same Figure 4 series demonstrating the widened jugular foramen caused by the glomus jugulare tumor. C: Axial bone-window CT with the orange arrow pointing to the markedly widened right jugular foramen and calliper measurement (1.04 cm) of the enlarged foramen, the hallmark of glomus jugulare. D: Coronal bone-window CT reconstruction from the same series with calliper measurements (1.26 cm, 4.01 mm) documenting the widened jugular foramen produced by the glomus jugulare tumor.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial T1-weighted MRI of the skull base in a patient with glomus jugulare; caption identifies a left soft tissue lesion with low T1 signal, lytic mastoid air cell destruction, and middle ear extension. Disease attribution is supported by the article title and in-text statement that findings were consistent with Class C glomus jugulare tumor. B: Axial T1-weighted post-gadolinium MRI showing a left skull base soft tissue lesion with heterogeneous avid enhancement, lytic mastoid air cell destruction, and middle ear extension. Caption and in-text mentions support glomus jugulare (Class C).

panels.figure_caption: (A) and (B): Axial T1-weighted (left) and T1-weighted post-gadolinium (right) MRI images of the skull base. The red arrows indicate a soft tissue lesion on the left side, which appears low signal on T1W (left) and shows heterogeneous, avid enhancement post-gadolinium (right). The lesion causes lytic destruction of the left mastoid air cells and extends into the middle ear cavity.
